title: Rational conjugacy of maximal split tori over any field
statement: Let $k$ be any field [def-weil-field]. Let $G$ be a smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] affine $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], geometrically connected (connected [def-weil-connected-scheme] after every field extension), and reductive: over an algebraic closure it has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. Here unipotent means that all geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful finite-dimensional representation. Write $\mathbf G_{m,k}=\operatorname{Spec}k[z,z^{-1}]$ with multiplication of units. A split torus is a group scheme isomorphic over $k$ to $\mathbf G_{m,k}^r$ for some integer $r\geq0$. A maximal split torus of $G$ is a closed split torus subgroup [def-weil-closed-immersion] maximal under inclusion among closed split torus subgroups defined over $k$. If $S_1,S_2\hookrightarrow G$ are maximal split tori, then there exists $g\in G(k)$ such that conjugation $c_g:G\to G$ restricts to an isomorphism $S_1\xrightarrow{\sim}S_2$ over $k$. Here $G(B)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}B,G)$ and $(c_g)_B(x)=g_Bxg_B^{-1}$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $B$. No perfectness, infinitude or algebraic closedness hypothesis is made on $k$; rank-zero tori are allowed.

source.place: Theorem 25.10, printed p.546, in Section 25(a) (G reductive over the arbitrary base field k). The conclusion is conjugacy by G(k), not just geometric conjugacy.

proof.text: First record the commuting case. If closed split tori $A,B\subseteq G$ commute after every algebra extension, multiplication $m:A\times_kB\to G$ is a homomorphism: $aba^{\prime}b^{\prime}=aa^{\prime}bb^{\prime}$. The product is again a coordinate split torus, hence affine of finite type by [lem-trf-lattice-torus-coordinates-action]. Apply [lem-sfb-affine-homomorphism-flat-image] to $m$, obtaining $A\times_kB\twoheadrightarrow I\hookrightarrow G$ with faithfully flat first map. By [lem-sfb-field-split-torus-flat-quotient], $I$ is a split torus over the same $k$. Both $A$ and $B$ factor through $I$ by restricting $m$ to $(a,1)$ and $(1,b)$. Thus if $A,B$ are maximal split tori of $G$, maximality gives $A=I=B$. These are subgroup-scheme factorizations; surjectivity on $k$-points is not asserted.

source.place: Theorems 3.34 and 12.9, pp.75,233--234; Definition 12.14, p.236. Commuting-case assembly used at the end of 25.10.

proof.text: If every closed split torus of $G$ is central, then $S_1,S_2$ commute, so step 1 gives $S_1=S_2$; take $g=1$. Otherwise [lem-sfb-field-parabolic-isotropy-criterion] gives a proper minimal parabolic $P$ over $k$. Its quotient $X=G/P$ is proper of finite type by that node, and has the rational point $q(1)$. By [lem-sfb-field-parabolic-quotient-rational-lift], $X$ carries the left multiplication action of $G$, the quotient map $q$ is equivariant, and its identity fibre is $P$ on every algebra.

source.place: Proposition 25.2, p.545; Theorem 25.9(b), p.546. Repairs the central split-torus case in the first two sentences of 25.10.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-rational-fixed-point] separately to the restricted actions of $S_i$ on $X$, for $i=1,2$. The hypotheses hold because $X$ is proper finite type and $q(1)\in X(k)$. Obtain rational fixed points $x_i$. By [lem-sfb-field-parabolic-quotient-rational-lift], choose $h_i\in G(k)$ with $q(h_i)=x_i$. For every commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $s\in S_i(A)$, equivariance and fixedness give $q(sh_i)=q(h_i)$, hence $q(h_i^{-1}sh_i)=q(1)$ after applying the left action of $h_i^{-1}$. The identity-fibre assertion gives $h_i^{-1}sh_i\in P(A)$. Taking the universal point of the affine $S_i$ shows that $R_i=h_i^{-1}S_ih_i$ factors as a subgroup scheme through $P$. Each $R_i$ remains maximal among split tori of $G$, since conjugation by $h_i$ is an inverse-preserving isomorphism carrying any larger split torus back to one containing $S_i$. It is therefore maximal in $P$ as well.

source.place: Theorem 25.10, middle sentences, p.546; Theorem 16.51, p.343; Theorem 25.9(b), p.546. The inverse in the conjugation is fixed by the displayed coset calculation.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-minimal-parabolic-split-centralizers] for the minimal $P$ and its maximal split tori $R_1,R_2$. Write $L_i=C_G(R_i)$ and choose $u\in(R_uP)(k)$ with $uL_1u^{-1}=L_2$. Since every torus is commutative, $R_1\subseteq L_1$, so $uR_1u^{-1}\subseteq L_2=C_G(R_2)$. The latter inclusion says exactly that $uR_1u^{-1}$ commutes with $R_2$ over every algebra. Both are maximal split tori of $G$, and step 1 yields $uR_1u^{-1}=R_2$. Put $g=h_2uh_1^{-1}\in G(k)$. Substituting $R_i=h_i^{-1}S_ih_i$ gives $gS_1g^{-1}=S_2$. The conjugation morphism constructed from multiplication, inverse and $g$ has inverse conjugation by $g^{-1}$, so its restriction is the asserted isomorphism over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme]. The same identities hold on all algebra points. The argument used no extra field hypothesis and also covers rank zero.

source.place: Theorem 25.6(b),(c), pp.545--546, with minimality correction (author errata); final sentences of 25.10, p.546, completed by the commuting-torus argument of step 1.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 25.10, p.546; assembly from 16.51,25.2,25.6,25.9, correcting two omissions: central split tori do not force a proper parabolic, and the centralizer statement needs a minimal parabolic. Commuting tori close the proof without dimension induction.
